why.title: Every witness, one wall
why.body: Each Canary keeps its own signed chain — deliberately. The hub is where they converge: one dashboard, one timeline, one place the household actually looks.

why.title: Local, like everything else here
why.body: A Raspberry Pi on your shelf. No cloud account, no subscription — witness data never has to leave the house.

why.title: It does things
why.body: A smoke-alarm cadence heard → a push that bypasses every silent phone. A tamper → the lights come on. A chain failure → you know in seconds.

why.title: Verified ✓ means verified
why.body: The integration pins each device's Ed25519 key and verifies every publish. The timeline's checkmark is a signature check, not a decoration.

hardware.title: One evening on the kitchen table
hardware.intro: A Raspberry Pi 4 or 5, a good microSD card, a vented case, wired ethernet if you can. Scrub it apart, then walk the build.

needs.note: Pi 5 works great — ~3 cameras at 10 fps if you later add Frigate
this card IS the computer's disk
15 W (Pi 4) / 27 W (Pi 5) — undervoltage is the classic mystery crash
any vented case; passive cooling is fine
e.g. a 7" 1024x600 IPS panel with USB touch — the hub runs headless by default, but with a screen it can show your dashboard (the “display” extra in self-setup)

steps.title: Start with the case
steps.note: Any vented case will do. A hub runs 24/7 — airflow is the whole spec.

steps.title: Seat the board
steps.note: Onto the posts, ports facing the openings. It should sit flat, no rock.

steps.title: Heatsink on the SoC
steps.note: Peel, align to the big square chip, press. Passive is plenty.

steps.title: The card is the computer
steps.note: Into the underside slot, label facing the board. Flash it first — Chapter 1 in the bench terminal below.

steps.title: Close it up
steps.note: Lid on until it clicks. Leave the SD slot reachable if you can.

steps.title: Wire it — ethernet first, power last
steps.note: Ethernet to your router, then USB-C. Power IS the switch; first boot takes up to 20 minutes.

chapters.title: 1 · Flash the card
chapters.intro: On your computer, card in a reader — or let Raspberry Pi Imager (Other specific-purpose OS → Home assistants) do all of this for you, verify included.

steps.note: Find the card — 59.5G in a reader. The only dangerous step on this page is getting this wrong.
Pi 5: same release, image haos_rpi5-64-{{haos}}.img.xz. The version is live from this page's snapshot.
Yours will differ — compare it against the SHA-256 on the release page. Never skip this.
Unpacks to a raw disk image.

steps.cmd: sudo dd if=haos_rpi4-64-{{haos}}.img of=/dev/sdb bs=4M conv=fsync status=progress
out: 2101346304 bytes (2.1 GB, 2.0 GiB) copied, 128 s, 16.4 MB/s
steps.note: dd erases /dev/sdb completely — triple-check. Then eject, and back to the build: Step 4.

chapters.title: 2 · First boot
chapters.intro: Card in, ethernet in, power last. First boot installs — up to 20 minutes. Watch for it:

out: 64 bytes from 192.168.1.87: icmp_seq=0 ttl=64 time=1.42 ms
64 bytes from 192.168.1.87: icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=1.11 ms
64 bytes from 192.168.1.87: icmp_seq=2 ttl=64 time=1.09 ms
3 packets transmitted, 3 packets received, 0.0% packet loss
steps.note: mDNS, same trick every Canary uses. Silent? Wait — first boot is genuinely slow, once.
It's up. Open http://homeassistant.local:8123, create the owner account (it lives only on the Pi) — that's onboarding.

entities.name: Witness Count
entities.desc: total witness records created (`witness_count`; signed `counts` topic)

entities.name: Chain Valid
entities.desc: ON only when the device reports its chain intact and the chain publish verified against the pinned key; unknown until a chain publish has been checked (`chain_valid`; signed `chain` topic)

entities.name: Online
entities.desc: device connectivity, from the `status` topic (`online`; unsigned)

entities.name: Die Temperature
entities.desc: chip die temperature, whole degrees (silicon, not room)

entities.name: Smoke Alarm Heard
entities.desc: binary sensors that latch ON when the mic matches an NFPA 72 T3 smoke or UL 2034 CO cadence, and clear about 30 seconds after the alarm stops

entities.name: CO Alarm Heard
entities.desc: binary sensors that latch ON when the mic matches an NFPA 72 T3 smoke or UL 2034 CO cadence, and clear about 30 seconds after the alarm stops

entities.name: Microphone Mute
